Title: Topo Bridge
Area: Master’s thesis, Pars University of Architecture and Art
Services: Dr. Mohammadreza Matini (supervisor), University of Art, Tehran, m.matini@art.ac.ir. Dr. Morteza Rahbar (advisor), Iran University of Science and Technology, rahbarm@iust.ac.ir
Project Introduction: In nature, morphogenesis is the process by which an organism develops its shape, from birth to maturity and across generations. The forms that survive put material only where it is needed. Topology optimization, a tool from structural engineering, can simulate this process and produce structures in which form and structure are the same thing.
Design Concept: Topo Bridge applies the method to a bridge for walking and cycling that links Chitgar Lake, on the north side, with Chitgar Forest Park to the south, in west Tehran. The design starts from simple volumes drawn along the paths people already use. Each segment is given its loads and supports, and the solver removes material until only an organic, branching structure remains. The optimized segments are then assembled into one bridge.
Project Summary: The decks follow the lines of force. They carry separate tracks for cyclists, runners and pedestrians, with places to gather and planted areas along the way, and they open where the structure divides. Two entrances reach the bridge from the north and four from the south.

Title: ESTA
Area: Design studio, Pars University of Architecture and Art
Services: Dr. Mohammadreza Matini, University of Art, Tehran, m.matini@art.ac.ir
Project Introduction: ESTA is a bridge made from a large number of loose elements. Instead of drawing the structure, the architect watches and adjusts how the elements pile up and lock together, at the scale of a single particle and at the scale of the whole bridge.
Design Concept: The element comes from Centaurea calcitrapa, a star thistle common across the Middle East, whose sharp spines catch on one another. Physical experiments showed that a star shape locks best into an arch. The final module has fourteen loosely connected spikes. Buttresses modelled on honey locust thorns anchor the aggregate on both banks. Loose aggregation kept failing in the computer, so the upper levels use chains of three modules, placed over rigid buttresses at the base. The result was verified in 3ds Max MassFX.
Project Summary: Inside the aggregate is a sequence of spaces: a viewpoint open to the outside, a larger room with a café, three lifts, and a gallery where light falls through the modules in shifting spots. Construction would follow four steps: supports and temporary arches, aggregation, interior spaces wrapped in single and chained modules, then more aggregation before the temporary arches come out.

Title: Porta Verde
Area: Design studio, team of ten, Politecnico di Milano
Services: Politecnico di Milano, Architectural Design Studio and Sustainable Building Technologies
Team: Mojtaba Mohammadi, Ali, Amr, Beantenew, Hanieh, Mobina, Padideh, Raha, Sima, Yared
Project Introduction: Porta Verde is an office and co-working building with a restaurant, set around a planted courtyard. Its form comes from a sequence of environmental moves. The mass is oriented for solar gain, lifted to make terraces where shadow analysis allows, adjusted to add roof courts for growing food, and carved at ground level so the site stays open and easy to cross.
Design Concept: The landscape is part of the program. Shade trees, fruit trees, a herb and vegetable garden, an outdoor café and a lawn make the courtyard a place to work, eat and rest. Inside, a growing wall continues the garden.
Project Summary: The team developed the timber structure from the overall frame down to wall sections and construction details.

Title: Expo Pavilion
Area: Design studio, team project, Pars University of Architecture and Art
Services: Dr. Mahmoud Golabchi, University of Tehran, golabchi@ut.ac.ir. Dr. Katayoun Taghizadeh, University of Tehran, ktaghizad@ut.ac.ir
Project Introduction: The Expo theme was “Connecting Minds, Creating the Future”. The team began with very different ideas and looked for what they shared. The answer was the tree, and above all its roots: many and different, deep and shallow, old and young, all working to keep one tree alive.
Design Concept: The tree is the cedar carved on the walls of Persepolis about 500 BC. It bears no fruit, so it is called free, and it stands for freedom in Iranian culture. Its roots spread across the whole site and continue inside the building.
Project Summary: The structure takes its logic from fine bone tissue, which is light and strong. It would be printed in large parts from a filament of bamboo mixed with PLA or PHA, stacked to form the shell, with the smell and touch of wood. Inside, tree-like supports take the place of ordinary walls, and solar panels on the shell power the building.

Title: Tsunawe
Area: Competition entry, team project, Jacques Rougerie Foundation
Services: Dr. Mahmoud Golabchi, University of Tehran, golabchi@ut.ac.ir. Dr. Katayoun Taghizadeh, University of Tehran, ktaghizad@ut.ac.ir
Project Introduction: Tsunamis put coastal towns and ports at risk, while rising seas and growing populations shrink the land left for living and farming. Tsunawe, a tranquil suspended seaport, is a settlement at sea designed for both problems.
Design Concept: The settlement protects itself by lifting its upper part above the water on a magnetic levitation system, so tsunami waves pass underneath. The upper part holds rings of buildings, green land and water channels, a soil-covered hill for trees and plants, and a landmark tower at the centre with health, shopping and other services.
Project Summary: The harbour sits below, where ships berth. In an emergency it can move out of danger and evacuate everyone on board. Waves, wind, tides and the sun power the whole system.

Title: Nodo Bovisa
Area: Design studio, team of five, Politecnico di Milano
Services: Prof. Massimo Tadi, Politecnico di Milano
Team: Mojtaba Mohammadi, Göksu Aktün, Chiara Berti, Ali Elsayed, Hanieh Farhad
Project Introduction: The project designs an extension of Nodo Bovisa in the north of Milan. To respect the needs of the node, the site is divided into three parts, and the solid volumes are hollowed out to make internal courtyards.
Design Concept: The volumes are separated along a central axis so the ground stays walkable, and they take on more complex shapes in response to the landscape. Following a study of the sun’s path, the residential volumes rise in steps of increasing height.
Project Summary: The towers are detailed with balconies and planter boxes on a cross-laminated timber structure.

Title: VoxGrowth
Area: Computational design workshop, IUST and Shanghai Institute of Visual Arts
Services: Dr. Morteza Rahbar, Iran University of Science and Technology, rahbarm@iust.ac.ir
Project Introduction: Differential growth happens when cells divide faster in some places than in others, usually along an edge. The edge grows longer than the surface it belongs to, so it buckles and curls, as in brain coral, plants and fungi.
Design Concept: In this computational design workshop the growth algorithm became a way of designing objects: pendant lights and furniture whose surfaces fold like living tissue.
Project Summary: Adding more behaviours to the algorithm produces a wider family of patterns, from tight coral-like folds to loose, open curves.

Title: The Green Oasis
Area: Urban design and building renovation studios, team of nine, Politecnico di Milano
Services: Prof. Angela Colucci and Sara Lodrini (urban design), Prof. Manuela Grecchi and Elena Bianchi (building renovation), Politecnico di Milano
Team: Mojtaba Mohammadi, Asma Aboudief, Chiara Berti, Ali Elsayed, Hanieh Farhad, Tanay Mahajan, Akmal Nasirov, Padideh Poormehrabi, Amr Tarek
Project Introduction: The studio, Living + Nature, asked for the regeneration of San Cristoforo in Milan and of Aldo Rossi’s former station there. Our team built the plan around community gardening: a hub where residents grow food together, share tools and knowledge, and meet.
Design Concept: Four goals shape the masterplan. Agriculture: community gardens and orchards. Ecology: ponds, wetland planting, an ecological park and a reshaped course for the Olona river. Infrastructure: green bridges over the Naviglio Grande and the railway, cycle paths and new links across the district. Public life: housing, play, sport and leisure for residents and visitors.
Project Summary: A main pedestrian spine runs from public to more private areas, with wave-shaped entrances along the promenade and aromatic and botanical gardens at its heart. In the renovation studio, the station becomes affordable housing with a community centre. Reversible interventions keep its volume and structure, modular apartments can grow over time, and terraces open every unit to the outside.
